common_name: Bobolink Blueberry (Vigorous Large-Fruited University of Florida Southern Highbush)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic, well-drained soil; Bobolink (FL03-291), patented by the University of Florida (US PP21,377), needs only about 200 hours of winter chill and leafs out early, so it is best suited to the mildest parts of zone 8b-9.

directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to keep the shallow root system cool and moist. Bobolink is a low-chill University of Florida southern highbush release carrying US Plant Patent PP21,377, prized for its strong upright vigor, abundant pollen production, and notably large berries (averaging roughly 2.75 grams) that form in loose, easy-to-strip clusters. It ripens mid-season, with first harvest around mid-to-late April near Gainesville, Florida, and performs reliably even after mild winters that leave many higher-chill varieties under-fruited. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and lightly again after harvest, and prune out older canes each winter to renew fruiting wood.
sources: Florida Foundation Seed Producers — Blueberry Variety Licensing
University of Florida IFAS — Blueberry Breeding Program

common_name: Raven Blueberry (Spreading Mid-Season University of Florida Southern Highbush)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Raven (FL05-627), patented by the University of Florida (US PP21,374), needs about 300 hours of winter chill and flowers later than most Florida releases, making it a good fit for zone 8b-9 gardens that want to spread out the bloom and harvest window.

directions: Plant in acidic, organically rich, well-drained soil and mulch heavily with pine bark to buffer the shallow root system from heat and drought. Raven is a University of Florida southern highbush release carrying US Plant Patent PP21,374, with a somewhat spreading habit that forms a dense canopy similar to the older 'Star' cultivar, and it produces exceptionally large berries with low acidity and mild flavor that hold their firmness on the bush well after ripening. It flowers later than most Florida cultivars, with roughly half its blooms open by early February, and ripens mid-season with first harvest around mid-to-late April near Gainesville. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and thin out old wood each winter to keep the dense canopy productive.
sources: Florida Foundation Seed Producers — Blueberry Variety Licensing
University of Florida IFAS — Blueberry Breeding Program

common_name: Sapphire Blueberry (Semi-Upright University of Florida Southern Highbush)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Sapphire, patented by the University of Florida (US PP11,829), has a stated chilling requirement of about 250 hours, putting it toward the lower-chill end of the southern highbush range.

directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark and keep heavily mulched to conserve moisture around the shallow root system. Sapphire is a University of Florida southern highbush blueberry carrying US Plant Patent PP11,829, grown as a semi-upright, somewhat spreading bush that bears medium-to-large fruit. It has been widely licensed for commercial production across both hemispheres, from the Southeast to South America, South Africa, and the EU. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune selectively each winter to keep light penetrating the canopy.
sources: Florida Foundation Seed Producers — Blueberry Variety Licensing
University of Florida IFAS — Blueberry Breeding Program

common_name: Southern Belle Blueberry (Firm Shippable University of Florida Southern Highbush)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic, well-drained soil; Southern Belle, patented by the University of Florida (US PP13,931), needs about 400 hours of winter chill, suiting zone 8-9 gardens.

directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) enriched with pine bark and kept well mulched to protect the shallow root system from Gulf South heat. Southern Belle is a University of Florida southern highbush blueberry, protected under US Plant Patent PP13,931, grown as an upright bush with a dense canopy that produces large, notably firm berries with excellent packing and shipping qualities. It ripens in mid-to-late spring, with first harvest around late April near Gainesville, Florida, and requires well-drained soil to perform at its best. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and lightly again after harvest, and prune out aging wood each winter to maintain fruiting vigor.
sources: Florida Foundation Seed Producers — Blueberry Variety Licensing
University of Florida IFAS — Blueberry Breeding Program

common_name: San Joaquin Blueberry (Mediterranean-Climate University of Florida Southern Highbush)

planting.note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic, well-drained soil; San Joaquin (FLX-1), patented by the University of Florida (US PP19,342), needs 400-500 hours of winter chill and was field-tested in California's San Joaquin Valley, performing best in dry, Mediterranean-type climates rather than humid Gulf South summers.

directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil and mulch heavily to keep the shallow root system cool, choosing an open, airy site since this cultivar is prone to disease pressure in humid climates. San Joaquin, bred by the University of Florida and carrying US Plant Patent PP19,342, is a vigorous, upright southern highbush selection that produces large, very firm, sweet berries ripening in early spring, around mid-to-late April near Gainesville, Florida. Despite its Florida breeding origin it is best adapted to desert or Mediterranean climates such as California's San Joaquin Valley, where drier conditions reduce the fungal disease pressure that limits its performance in the humid Southeast. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, and prune out old wood each winter to maintain yield.
sources: Florida Foundation Seed Producers — Blueberry Variety Licensing
University of Florida IFAS — Blueberry Breeding Program
